title: Report on Fort McMurray RCMP involved shooting says nothing could have been done differently
article: In the early morning hours of March 16, 2011, Const. Marshall broke the glass door of a Fort McMurray apartment complex with the butt of his shotgun and proceeded down a hallway toward a suite where shots had reportedly been fired.
Four other officers carrying 9-mm pistols followed. Marshall past a short wall projecting into the hallway, then noticed Ahmad Abdallah in the corner, holding a beer in his left hand.
The 24-year-old raised a pistol and fired at Marshall, who returned a bullet with his shotgun, striking Abdullah on the left side.

According to a recent fatality inquiry report, Abdullah fired again, this time striking Const. Curnew in her butt, the bullet exiting through her right thigh. Despite her injury, Curnew fired back with her pistol, striking Abdallah in the back of the chest.
One of Abdullah's bullets also struck Marshall, but it was stopped by his police radio. A third round fired before Abdullah's death was found in an adjacent vacant suite.

Before police arrived at the scene, Abdullah got into an argument during a visit with of the residents of the apartment building. He refused to take off his shoes and produced a handgun, pointing it at a man and stated, "I could hurt you."

A frightened woman inside the apartment suite locked herself in a bathroom and called 911. While she was on the phone, Abdullah fired his gun twice into the floor. The shots were heard on the 911 recording.
Toxicology results showed Abdullah had a blood alcohol concentration of 80 mg/100 ml. His blood and liver also showed high levels of methamphetamine.
In the report, Provincial Court Judge Jim Jacques said the officers involved did precisely what they should have done under the circumstances.

"They responded promptly, intelligently and bravely to a potential life-threatening situation," said Jacques. "It is not unlikely that Const. Marshall and Const. Curnew saved not only their own lives, but those of their fellow officers by reacting rapidly and accurately to a deadly threat."
Jacques had no recommendations that would prevent a similar incident from occurring.
